opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that, for us, they're not really two separate things anymore.

When we started SGLang, the focus was serving: how do you make large language model inference fast, efficient, and cheap, whether that's through better scheduling, prefix caching, structured generation, or getting more out of the hardware. That's still a big part of what we do. But as the field moved, especially with reasoning models and agentic workloads, reinforcement learning became one of the main ways people improve models after pretraining. And if you look at an RL training loop today, a huge portion of the time and compute goes into rollouts, which means generating lots of samples from the current policy. That's inference. So the RL system is only as good as the inference engine sitting inside it.

We saw many teams building RL pipelines where the rollout side was kind of an afterthought, and that became the bottleneck. You'd have very long generations, highly variable output lengths, multi-turn interactions with tools or environments, and you need to sync weights between the trainer and the inference engine over and over again. All of those are fundamentally inference-system problems. Since we'd already spent years optimizing exactly those things in SGLang, it felt natural to build the RL infrastructure on top of it rather than have people glue things together themselves.

There's also a feedback loop going the other direction. When we build Miles and run real RL workloads at scale, we discover requirements that pure serving never surfaced, like fast weight updates, deterministic or reproducible sampling, better support for very long-horizon agent rollouts, and tighter consistency between what the trainer computes and what the inference engine produces. Those improvements then flow back into SGLang and make it better for everyone, including people who only use it for serving.

So from my perspective, it's one stack. Inference is the engine, and RL is one of the most demanding and important workloads that engine has to support. Doing both lets us co-design them, and I think that co-design is where a lot of the real efficiency gains are going to come from over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response describes inference and reinforcement learning as connected parts of one stack, but does not identify them as the two stages of AI infrastructure closest to users.

r002.rationale: The response says co-designing inference and RL can improve efficiency, but does not frame their development as a starting point toward the full capability to produce AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that inference and reinforcement learning stopped being separate problems about two years ago, and we're just building the infrastructure to match that reality.

When we started SGLang, the goal was pretty narrow: make LLM serving fast and programmable. RadixAttention for prefix caching, a frontend language for structured generation, that kind of thing. It was an inference engine, and we thought of it as an inference engine.

But then post-training changed. If you look at how a frontier model gets trained today, the expensive part is no longer the pretraining loop, it's the RL loop. And inside an RL loop, most of the wall-clock time and most of the compute is spent generating rollouts. You sample thousands of trajectories, you score them, you do a small update, and you sample again. That sampling step is just inference. So the thing that was supposed to be our "serving" engine was suddenly sitting in the middle of the training pipeline.

Once you see that, the question becomes: who owns the boundary between the trainer and the rollout engine? For a long time the answer was "nobody," and it showed. Weight syncing was slow and brittle. The sampler and the trainer disagreed about numerics, so your policy was learning from samples a slightly different model produced. KV cache was thrown away between generations. Multi-turn and agentic rollouts, where the model calls tools and waits on an environment, didn't fit the batch abstraction at all. Every team ended up writing a thin, fragile glue layer and then complaining about it.

Miles is our attempt to own that boundary. It's the RL side of the same stack. We built it on top of SGLang rather than beside it, so the rollout engine and the trainer share the same assumptions about weights, memory, and scheduling. That lets us do things that are hard when the two pieces come from different projects: fast in-place weight updates without tearing down the engine, keeping prefix caches alive across RL steps, scheduling asynchronous and partial rollouts for agents that spend most of their time waiting on tool calls, and keeping the training and inference numerics close enough that the off-policy drift is something you measure instead of something you discover.

There's also a practical, slightly selfish reason. The people pushing SGLang hardest were increasingly RL teams, and their feature requests were things like "I need to swap weights every thirty seconds" or "I need to pause a generation mid-sequence and resume it later." If we only thought of ourselves as a serving project, those requests look weird. If we think of ourselves as the generation engine for the whole model lifecycle, they're the most important features we can build.

So I'd frame it less as doing two things and more as refusing to pretend they're two things. Inference is how you serve a model, and it's also how you train the next one. We want one engine that's good at both, and Miles is how we make sure the training side actually gets the attention it needs.

r001.rationale: The response discusses inference and reinforcement learning as connected parts of model serving and training, but does not identify them as the two stages closest to users.

r002.rationale: The response describes building a shared inference and RL stack for the model lifecycle, but does not frame these efforts as a starting point toward the full capability to produce AI.

astra-6.text:
For me, these are two closely connected parts of the same problem. SGLang focuses on making inference efficient, and inference is a major component of reinforcement learning for language models. The model generates responses, we evaluate those responses, and then we use that feedback to update the model. That cycle repeats, so the efficiency of generation has a direct impact on how quickly we can train and experiment.

But a fast inference engine alone isn’t enough. You also need infrastructure to coordinate generation, reward computation, training, and the movement of updated weights back into the inference engine. That’s the role of Miles: making those pieces work together efficiently.

Working on both lets us improve the whole loop. The reinforcement learning workload tells us what the inference engine needs to support, and improvements in inference let us run more experiments or generate more experience with the same resources. So I see them as complementary layers of infrastructure.

r001.rationale: The response connects inference and reinforcement learning, but does not identify them as the two AI infrastructure stages closest to users.

r002.rationale: It describes improving the inference and reinforcement-learning loop, but does not frame their development as a starting point toward building the full capability to produce AI.

sol-6.1.text:
To me, they’re two parts of the same problem. With SGLang, we’re focused on making inference efficient. But in reinforcement learning, generating responses is a major part of the training process. The model produces outputs, gets feedback, and then updates. So inference is actually inside the training loop.

That means improvements to inference can directly improve reinforcement learning. But you also need infrastructure to coordinate generation, training, and moving updated weights back to the inference engines. That’s the motivation for Miles: making that whole loop work efficiently.

Working on both lets us optimize across that boundary. What we learn from reinforcement learning tells us what inference needs to support, and better inference makes reinforcement learning faster and more practical.

r001.rationale: The response says inference and reinforcement learning are connected parts of one problem and explains their interaction, but does not identify them as the two stages closest to users.

r002.rationale: It describes improving the inference–training loop through SGLang and Miles, but does not frame this work as a starting point toward building the full capability to produce AI.
